questions.stem: In the circular flow of income model, real flows and money flows move in opposite directions. Which is a real flow?
options: Wages paid by businesses to households
Spending by households on goods and services
Taxes paid by businesses to the government
Labour supplied by households to businesses
questions.explanation: Real flows are the factors of production and the goods and services they produce. Wages, spending and taxes are money flows that pay for those real flows.

questions.stem: In the circular flow model, the resources (factor) market is where:
options: businesses sell finished goods and services to households for spending
the financial sector lends household savings to businesses for investment
the government collects taxes from households and businesses
households sell factors of production to businesses in return for incomes
questions.explanation: In the resources market households supply land, labour, capital and enterprise and receive rent, wages, interest and profit. Finished goods and services are exchanged in the goods market.

questions.stem: The simplest two-sector circular flow model assumes that:
options: exports always equal imports, so the overseas sector can be ignored
households spend all their income and there is no saving, government or trade
businesses save all their profits and households borrow to fund spending
the government collects taxes but does not spend any of the revenue it raises
questions.explanation: With only households and businesses, all income is spent on output and all spending becomes income, so the flow stays constant. Adding the financial, government and overseas sectors introduces withdrawals and injections.

questions.stem: What is the main difference between a closed and an open circular flow model?
options: An open model includes the overseas sector, with exports and imports
A closed model includes the government sector, with taxes and spending
An open model leaves out the financial sector and household saving
A closed model shows only money flows and leaves out real flows
questions.explanation: A closed economy has no trade, so it has four sectors at most. The open five-sector model adds the overseas sector, with exports as an injection and imports as a withdrawal.

questions.stem: Why do economists treat the circular flow of income as a model rather than a full description of the economy?
options: It predicts the exact size of GDP in each future quarter
It simplifies a complex economy with assumptions so key relationships can be seen
It records every single transaction in the economy exactly as the ABS measures it
It applies only to economies with no government, banks or foreign trade
questions.explanation: Models leave out detail on purpose, grouping millions of decisions into a few sectors and flows. This makes cause and effect visible, but conclusions depend on the assumptions made.

questions.stem: In the five-sector circular flow model, the withdrawals (leakages) are:
options: investment, government spending and exports
consumption, wages and profits
savings, investment and exports
savings, taxation and imports
questions.explanation: Withdrawals are income not passed on as spending on domestic output: income saved, paid in tax or spent on imports. Investment, government spending and exports are the matching injections.

questions.stem: Which is an injection into Australia's circular flow of income?
options: A worker pays income tax through the PAYG system
A mining company buys new machinery for a Queensland mine
A household puts part of its weekly pay into a savings account
A retailer buys a shipment of televisions made in South Korea
questions.explanation: Business investment adds spending that does not come from households' current income. Saving, imports and tax all take income out of the flow.

questions.stem: The circular flow of income is in equilibrium when:
options: household consumption equals household income
total injections equal total withdrawals
savings equal investment and taxes equal government spending
exports equal imports in every period
questions.explanation: The flow stays the same size when I + G + X equals S + T + M in total. Each pair need not balance; for example, a budget deficit can be offset by savings exceeding investment.

questions.stem: In a period, S = $90b, T = $120b, M = $100b, I = $100b, G = $130b and X = $80b. Which statement is correct?
options: The flow is in equilibrium, even though no pair of injection and withdrawal is equal
The flow will contract, because exports are less than imports
The flow will expand, because government spending exceeds taxation
The flow cannot be in equilibrium, because savings differ from investment
questions.explanation: Withdrawals total 90 + 120 + 100 = $310b and injections total 100 + 130 + 80 = $310b, so the flow is stable. Equilibrium needs only the totals to match, not each pair.

questions.stem: Injections total $420 billion and withdrawals total $445 billion. Other things being equal, the circular flow will:
options: contract, as more income leaves the flow than is added to it
expand, as withdrawals are being saved for future spending
stay the same, as withdrawals and injections are close in size
expand, as businesses respond to rising stocks by producing more
questions.explanation: When withdrawals exceed injections, spending on domestic output falls, so production, income and employment fall until a new equilibrium is reached. Unsold stock leads firms to cut output, not raise it.

questions.stem: In the five-sector model, the financial sector's main role is to:
options: collect taxes from businesses and pay transfer payments to households in need
set the prices of goods and services sold in the goods market
buy goods and services produced in other countries
channel household savings into loans that fund investment and spending
questions.explanation: Banks and other financial institutions take in savings, a withdrawal, and lend them out, which can return them as investment, an injection. Taxes and transfers are the government sector's role.

questions.stem: Aggregate demand is calculated as:
options: C + S + T + (X - M)
C + I + G + X + M
S + T + M - (I + G + X)
C + I + G + (X - M)
questions.explanation: Aggregate demand is total spending on Australian-produced goods and services: consumption, investment, government spending and net exports. Imports are subtracted because that spending goes to foreign producers.

questions.stem: In a year, C = $1,200b, I = $450b, G = $500b, X = $560b and M = $510b. Aggregate demand is:
options: $2,710 billion
$2,200 billion
$3,220 billion
$2,150 billion
questions.explanation: Aggregate demand = 1,200 + 450 + 500 + (560 - 510) = $2,200b. Adding imports instead of subtracting them gives $3,220b.

questions.stem: Gross domestic product (GDP) is best defined as:
options: the market value of all final goods and services produced in a country in a period
the total value of all goods and services sold, including intermediate inputs
the total income earned by Australian residents anywhere in the world
the value of goods and services exported by a country in a year
questions.explanation: GDP counts final output only, to avoid counting inputs twice. Because spending on output equals the income it generates, aggregate demand and GDP measure the same flow.

questions.stem: Why does a rise in aggregate demand usually lead to a rise in GDP?
options: Higher spending raises prices, and GDP measures only changes in the price level
Extra spending is saved by firms, which adds directly to GDP
Imports rise with spending, and imports are added to GDP
Firms produce more to meet the extra spending, raising output and incomes
questions.explanation: Spending on output is income to producers, so more spending leads firms to expand production and hire more workers. Imports are a withdrawal and are subtracted, not added.

questions.stem: Where would a student find official quarterly figures for Australia's GDP?
options: The Australian Taxation Office annual report
The Productivity Commission's inquiry reports
The Australian Bureau of Statistics national accounts
The Reserve Bank of Australia's cash rate announcement
questions.explanation: The ABS publishes Australian National Accounts each quarter, including GDP and its expenditure components. The RBA uses these data but does not produce them.

questions.stem: The economic (business) cycle describes:
options: the steady long-run rise in the economy's productive capacity over decades
the yearly pattern of government budget announcements
recurring rises and falls in the level of economic activity over time
the circular movement of money between households and businesses
questions.explanation: Economies move through booms, slowdowns, downturns and recoveries around their long-run growth path. The circular flow shows how money moves; the cycle shows how the size of that flow changes.

questions.stem: During a boom in the economic cycle, which conditions are most likely?
options: Falling incomes, falling prices and spare capacity across most industries
Falling investment as firms cut production
Rising employment and output, with growing pressure on prices
Rising unemployment and falling business confidence
questions.explanation: In a boom spending grows quickly, firms hire more and capacity becomes stretched, which pushes up prices. Rising unemployment and spare capacity mark a downturn.

questions.stem: To reduce the fluctuations of the economic cycle during a downturn, the government could:
options: cut its spending to encourage households to save more
increase tariffs so that exports rise
increase its spending or cut taxes to add to aggregate demand
raise taxes to reduce the size of the budget deficit and government debt
questions.explanation: Higher government spending is an injection and lower taxes reduce a withdrawal, so both expand the flow when private spending is weak. Raising taxes or cutting spending would deepen a downturn.

questions.stem: During a downturn, worried households all try to save a larger share of their incomes. Using the circular flow model, the paradox of thrift predicts that:
options: total saving rises, so investment and output also rise quickly
incomes rise, as banks lend the extra savings to households
imports rise, as households replace local goods with foreign ones
spending and incomes fall, so total saving may not rise at all
questions.explanation: Saving more is sensible for one household, but if all do it, spending falls, firms cut output and incomes fall, so total saving may not rise. This fallacy of composition shows that what holds for one need not hold for all.

questions.stem: The paradox of thrift is an example of the fallacy of composition because:
options: what is sensible for one household can harm the economy when all do it
saving is always harmful to both households and the economy
households cannot save unless the government runs a surplus
what is true for the economy must be true for each household
questions.explanation: One household saving more is better off, but all households saving more cut total spending and incomes. Saving also funds investment in the long run, so it is not always harmful.

questions.stem: The government cuts personal income tax rates. In the circular flow model, the most likely effect is:
options: a smaller withdrawal, raising disposable income, spending and the flow
a larger injection, as tax revenue is spent on public infrastructure projects
a smaller injection, reducing the size of the flow
no change, as taxation is not part of the circular flow model
questions.explanation: Taxation is a withdrawal, so lower tax leaves households more income to spend, raising consumption and aggregate demand. Government spending, not tax, is the injection.

questions.stem: The government pays a new subsidy to renewable energy producers. In the circular flow model this is most likely to:
options: increase withdrawals, as subsidies are paid for by taxes
reduce imports by making foreign energy more expensive
reduce aggregate supply in the renewable energy industry
increase injections and encourage more production in that industry
questions.explanation: A subsidy is government spending that lowers producers' costs, encouraging expansion. It is funded from revenue, but the subsidy itself adds to the flow and to supply in the industry.

questions.stem: One basis point is equal to:
options: 0.1 of a percentage point
1 per cent of the cash rate
one percentage point
0.01 of a percentage point
questions.explanation: Interest rate changes are often stated in basis points, with 100 basis points making one percentage point. A 25 basis point change is a quarter of a percentage point.

questions.stem: The cash rate rises from 3.60% to 3.85%. This change is:
options: 2.5 basis points, or 0.025 of a percentage point
0.25 basis points, or 25 per cent
25 basis points, or 0.25 of a percentage point
25 percentage points, or 0.25 basis points
questions.explanation: The rise is 3.85 - 3.60 = 0.25 percentage points, which is 25 basis points. Basis points measure changes in rates, with 100 basis points per percentage point.

questions.stem: An interest rate rises from 2.0% to 2.5%. Which statement is correct?
options: It rose by 50 percentage points, or 0.5 basis points, a 25 per cent increase
It rose by 0.5 percentage points, or 50 basis points, a 25 per cent increase
It rose by 0.5 per cent, or 5 basis points, a 50 per cent increase
It rose by 25 percentage points, or 50 basis points, a 0.5 per cent increase
questions.explanation: The difference is 0.5 percentage points, or 50 basis points. As a proportion of the original rate, 0.5 / 2.0 = 25 per cent, which is why percentage points and per cent must not be confused.

questions.stem: The Reserve Bank of Australia lowers the cash rate. In the circular flow model, the most likely effect is:
options: higher loan repayments, which reduce household spending
lower borrowing costs, which encourage consumption and investment
higher returns on savings, which encourage households to save more
an appreciation of the dollar, which raises export revenue
questions.explanation: Lower interest rates make borrowing cheaper and saving less rewarding, so consumption and investment, an injection, tend to rise and the flow expands. A lower rate also tends to depreciate the dollar, not appreciate it.

questions.stem: The RBA raises the cash rate by 50 basis points while the government increases its spending on infrastructure. In the circular flow model:
options: the effects partly offset, as the rate rise cuts private spending and G adds to it
both measures expand the flow, as higher rates raise savings and investment
both measures contract the flow, as government spending is a withdrawal
the rate rise has no effect, as it is less than one percentage point
questions.explanation: A higher cash rate tends to reduce consumption and investment, while extra government spending is an injection. The net effect depends on the relative size of each change.

questions.stem: Aggregate supply refers to:
options: the total spending on goods and services by all sectors of the economy in a period
the quantity of goods and services imported from overseas
the total savings available to the financial sector
the total quantity of goods and services firms are willing and able to produce
questions.explanation: Aggregate supply is the economy's total output of goods and services, which depends on the quantity and quality of resources and technology. Total spending is aggregate demand.

questions.stem: Higher skilled immigration increases the size of Australia's labour force. The most likely effect is:
options: an increase in aggregate supply and an outward shift of the PPC
a fall in aggregate supply, as more workers compete for jobs
an inward shift of the PPC, as resources must be shared more widely
a movement along the PPC towards more capital goods
questions.explanation: More workers mean more labour resources, so the economy can produce more and its production possibility curve shifts out. Migrants also spend their incomes, adding to aggregate demand.

questions.stem: A wave of innovation lets Australian businesses produce more with the same resources. Which links in the economy are most likely?
options: Aggregate supply falls, as fewer workers are needed for the same output
The PPC stays still, as only the quantity of resources can shift it
Only aggregate demand changes, as businesses spend more on technology
Aggregate supply rises, the PPC shifts out, and growth and employment can rise
questions.explanation: Innovation raises productivity, increasing productive capacity, which is shown by an outward PPC shift. This allows higher output and incomes, and new industries can create jobs even if some roles disappear.

questions.stem: Consumer confidence falls sharply as households fear job losses. In the circular flow model, the most likely effect is:
options: consumption rises as households spend before prices change
investment rises as firms expect lower wage costs
imports rise as households buy more overseas goods
saving rises and consumption falls, so the flow contracts
questions.explanation: Worried households cut spending and save more, increasing withdrawals relative to injections. Firms facing weaker sales cut output and may also postpone investment.

questions.stem: Economic conditions in a major trading partner of Australia deteriorate sharply. The most likely effect on Australia's circular flow is:
options: a fall in exports, an injection, which contracts the flow
a fall in imports, a withdrawal, which contracts the flow
a rise in exports, as the partner buys cheaper Australian goods
no effect, as foreign conditions affect only the overseas sector
questions.explanation: Lower incomes in the partner country reduce its demand for Australian exports, so injections fall and Australian output and incomes fall. The overseas sector is linked to the rest of the flow through trade.

questions.stem: The Australian dollar depreciates sharply against other currencies. Other things being equal, the most likely effect on the circular flow is:
options: exports fall and imports rise, so net exports and the flow decrease
exports and imports both rise by the same amount, so the flow is unchanged
savings rise as households hold Australian dollars for longer
exports rise and imports fall, so net exports and the flow increase
questions.explanation: A lower dollar makes Australian goods cheaper for foreigners and imports dearer for Australians, raising an injection and reducing a withdrawal. A higher dollar would have the opposite effect.

questions.stem: The minimum wage is increased. Which outcome best describes the possible effects on economic flows?
options: Low-paid workers may spend more, but higher costs may reduce some firms' hiring
Consumption must fall, as businesses pass on the full cost to households
Investment must rise, as firms replace all low-paid workers with machines
There is no effect on the flow, as wages are a transfer within one sector
questions.explanation: Higher wages raise the incomes of low-paid workers, who tend to spend most of their income, adding to consumption. Higher labour costs can also squeeze profits or reduce hiring, so the overall effect depends on the size of the increase.

questions.stem: Retail sales growth slows and business investment falls for several quarters. These data suggest that:
options: the economy is booming and inflation pressures are rising
injections are rising faster than withdrawals
aggregate demand is weakening and the circular flow is contracting
aggregate supply is falling because of a shortage of resources
questions.explanation: Retail sales reflect consumption, and investment is an injection, so falls in both indicate weaker spending and a slowing economy. A boom would show strong sales and investment.
